events.explanation: The `Series.first` method was removed in pandas 3.0. The notebook uses it to select the first 11 days of a time-series indexed by datetime. The equivalent modern API is to slice with `loc` up to the first timestamp plus a `Timedelta`.
events.diff:

+++ cell 4 (after)
@@ -1,2 +1,2 @@
 ts = pd.Series(range(6), index=dates.values)
-print(ts.first('11D').tolist())
+print(ts.loc[:ts.index[0] + pd.Timedelta('11D')].tolist())

sources.content:
Powered by Discourse, best viewed with JavaScript enabled [...] Thanks for reporting, @Reederey87  
A GItHub issue was opened a couple weeks ago about this. You can see updates here.

I raised a PR to fix this which has now been merged: handle deprecation of pandas.Series.dt.to\_pydatetime() calls and suppress their FutureWarnings by ned2 · Pull Request #4379 · plotly/plotly.py · GitHub

So this should be resolved in the next Plotly release.

### Related topics [...] This is due to a change in the Pandas API for the behaviour of `pandas.Series.dt.to_pydatetime`, which Plotly (not Dash) uses internally. Unfortunately as an end user the only thing we can do is suppress the `FutureWarning`. It’s something that will have to be addressed in the Plotly package.

# Pandas Series dt.weekofyear Method | Get Week of Year in Pandas Series

Last Updated : 11 Jul, 2025

The dt.weekofyear attribute returns a Series containing the week ordinal of the year in the underlying data of the given series object.

### Example [...] ### Example

 Python3  ````
 import pandas as pd sr = pd. Series(['2012-10-21 09:30','2019-7-18 12:30','2008-02-2 10:30','2010-4-22 09:25','2019-11-8 02:22']) idx =['Day 1', 'Day 2', 'Day 3', 'Day 4', 'Day 5'] sr. index = idx sr = pd. to_datetime(sr) result = sr. dt. weekofyear print(result)
```` 

Output:

weekofyear attribute output

## Syntax

> Syntax: Series.dt.weekofyear 
>
> Parameter:None 
>
> Returns: Series containing the week ordinal [...] Python3  ````
 # importing pandas as pd import pandas as pd # Creating the Series sr = pd. Series(pd. date_range('2012-12-12 12:12', periods = 5, freq = 'M')) # Creating the index idx =['Day 1', 'Day 2', 'Day 3', 'Day 4', 'Day 5'] # set the index sr. index = idx # Print the series print(sr)
```` 

Output :

Now we will use the Series.dt.weekofyear attribute to return the week ordinal of the year in the underlying data of the given Series object.

This logic is expanded to accessing the underlying pandas ExtensionArray through `.array` (or `.values` depending on the dtype) as well (GH 61925). sources.title: Migration guide for the new string data type (pandas 3.0) — pandas 3.0.6 documentation
sources.content:
First, in many cases it can be sufficient to remove the specific data type, and let pandas do the inference. But if you want to be specific, you can specify the `"str"` dtype:

```
>>> pd. Series(["a", "b", "c"], dtype = "str")
```

This is actually compatible with pandas 2.x as well, since in pandas < 3, `dtype="str"` was essentially treated as an alias for object dtype.

Attention [...] ```
>>> ser = pd. Series(["a", "b", None], dtype = "str")>>> ser =2.5 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------TypeError Traceback (most recent call last)...TypeError: Invalid value '2.5' for dtype 'str'. Value should be a string or missing value, got 'float' instead.
```

If you relied on the flexible nature of object dtype being able to hold any Python object, but your initial data was inferred as strings, your code might be impacted by this change. [...] ```
 # NEW behavior in pandas 3>>> pd. options. future. infer_string = True>>> ser = pd. Series([1.5, np. nan])>>> ser. astype("str") 01.5 1 NaN dtype: str>>> ser. astype("str"). to_numpy() array(['1.5', nan], dtype = object)
```
